title: Choosing a spouse
hook: four honest reasons people marry, and the one a hadith puts first

segments.voice: Yesterday, taklif, and your line: now it counts. Did one responsibility get your full attention? The child is grown. Today a new part of the path begins: marriage and home. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-seven.

A list, written before anyone has met. Steady income? Good family? Attractive? Gets along with my mother? These days some of that list lives inside apps, as filters you can slide up and down. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari makes a list like this too, and it's surprisingly frank about it. It doesn't pretend people marry for spiritual reasons alone. It names four reasons, out loud, and then it points at one of them and says: that one. Today: which one, and why a second hadith adds a word beside it.
screen: `A LIST, BEFORE ANYONE MEETS.` → `FOUR REASONS, NAMED OUT LOUD.` → `THEN: THAT ONE.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in paraphrase. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said: a woman is married for four things: her wealth, her family standing, her beauty, and her religion. Choose the one with religion, and you will prosper. Then he adds a sharp Arabic phrase, taribat yadak, which literally means may your hands be covered in dust. Here it works like a nudge: pay attention, get this one right. Notice what the hadith doesn't do. It doesn't call wealth, family or beauty bad. It names them plainly. It just won't let them sit at the top of the list. Second, character. A hadith in Jami' at-Tirmidhi speaks to a family receiving a proposal, in paraphrase: if someone comes to you whose religion and character please you, then marry. The Arabic for character is khuluq: the way a person actually is, on a bad day, when nobody's grading them. Put the two hadith side by side and you have today's line: faith and character first. Third, it runs both ways. One hadith speaks about choosing a wife. The other speaks about accepting a husband. The same measure falls on both sides. Fourth, what that looks like up close. Not a title. Not how loudly someone talks about religion. It shows in small things: how someone treats the person serving their food, whether they keep a promise that cost them something, how they speak about their parents, whether they keep their prayers on an ordinary weekday. The filters ask what someone has. These two hadith ask who someone is.
screen: `WEALTH, FAMILY, BEAUTY, RELIGION.` · `CHOOSE RELIGION: TARIBAT YADAK.` · `RELIGION AND CHARACTER PLEASE YOU.` · `WHO SOMEONE IS, NOT WHAT THEY HAVE.`

segments.voice: The practice: think about good character. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone whose character you trust. Not the most impressive person you know; the most dependable. What do they actually do? Keep their word? Speak kindly about people who aren't in the room? Choose one of those things and hold it. Then turn it around, gently: where does your own character already show like that, and where would you like it to? If you pray, you can ask for good character in your own words. If not, just keep the picture. The bell holds the time.
Choosing a spouse. Four reasons people marry, named honestly, and two put first: faith and character. Today's word.
Your line: character first. Today, notice one person's character before their résumé. Tomorrow, asking permission. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Muslims looking for a spouse, and their families, cite the hadith in Bukhari and Tirmidhi to put faith and character ahead of wealth, family standing and looks.

trapdoor: what you thought: a dating checklist.
what it means: four honest reasons people marry, with faith and character put first, on both sides.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari's four reasons ending 'choose the one with religion, taribat yadak', read with Tirmidhi's 'religion and character' (khuluq) for a proposal.
